key_facts: Council Bill 245 is being considered for final consideration and passage.
The bill involves a proposed rezoning of the property at 2423–2490 South University in Council District six from GMC-3 (General Urban Mixed Use Annex) to GRX-5 (General Urban Residential Mixed Use).
GRX-5 allows buildings up to 70 feet in height compared to the current 45 feet under GMC-3.
The property is located on the westernmost edge of Council District six in the University Park neighborhood.
The applicant is 100% owned by Knowlton of Colorado, who recently acquired the property formerly owned by the University of Denver and Colorado Seminary.
The property is approximately 75,000 square feet.
The Planning Board recommended support of the application with a unanimous 9–0 vote on March 5th.
It was forwarded to City Council after passing the Land Use Transportation Committee on March 25th.
A legal protest petition signed by 20% of landowners within a 200-foot buffer zone has been filed, requiring a supermajority of 10 affirmative votes for the bill to pass.
Public outreach included signs posted on the property and correspondence received from both supporters and opponents.
The project aligns with the University Park Neighborhood Plan and Blueprint Denver, promoting mixed-use development and enhanced transit corridors.
University Boulevard is identified as an enhanced transit corridor in Blueprint Denver.
The site is designated as urban residential and is part of the Ivy Towers district in the University Park Plan.
The proposed development includes 236 rental housing units, 25,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and parking below grade, exceeding code requirements.
Architectural renderings depict a building with setbacks, landscaped outdoor spaces, and sensitivity to the surrounding neighborhood.
A traffic study estimated minimal impact on existing traffic volumes, noting that the project would generate about 100 vehicles per hour during peak times.
Neighbors raised concerns about increased traffic, reduced sunlight, and potential negative effects on property values and neighborhood character.
The developer has committed to working with the neighborhood on design details and addressing specific concerns like solar shading and traffic access points.
There is significant opposition from the neighborhood, particularly from single-family homeowners directly behind the property.

Supporters argue that the rezoning reflects the vision of the 2008 University Park Neighborhood Plan, which recommends moderate density (3 to 5 stories), and supports walkable, pedestrian-friendly development.
Opponents claim there has been insufficient justification for the rezoning since the 2010 zoning code update and question the predictability of city planning decisions.
The developer has exceeded minimum parking requirements and aims to avoid surface parking to maintain a pedestrian-friendly environment.
Underground parking is expected to cost approximately $25,000 per space, adding considerable financial burden to the project.
If approved, the project will be subject to further studies, including traffic, wastewater, and utility assessments during the administrative site development plan stage.
The University of Denver supports the rezoning as it aligns with their ongoing investments in the area and enhances the University and Evans corridors.
The neighborhood's engagement and community discussions were extensive, including petitions, meetings, and public forums.
The current zoning (GMC-3) was adopted in 2010 after collaborative efforts between the city and the neighborhood, aiming for predictable standards.
The proposed GRX-5 zoning is more restrictive than GMC-3 regarding certain commercial uses, such as auto emissions and service repair labs.
City Council members expressed varied opinions, with some emphasizing the need for adherence to the neighborhood plan and others supporting the development’s potential benefits.
The rezoning debate centered on whether the change in ownership and assembling the entire block constituted a valid 'change in circumstances' justifying the zoning amendment.
During the public hearing, speakers included residents, developers, architects, and neighborhood representatives, highlighting both pros and cons of the proposal.
The vote required 10 affirmative votes due to the legal protest and passed with 13 votes in favor.
